# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and businesses. This comparison is beneficial for organizations looking to switch from Slack to Element, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and cost-effectiveness. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows full data ownership, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise for setup, whereas Slack is relatively straightforward.
* Scalability: Slack is more scalable due to its cloud-based infrastructure, while Element's scalability depends on the self-hosted server.
* Integration: Element has native integration with the Matrix protocol, while Slack has a wider range of third-party integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of third-party integrations
* Scalable cloud-based infrastructure
* Mobile apps for on-the-go access
* Limited data ownership and control
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* Full data ownership and control
* Native integration with the Matrix protocol
* Customizable and extensible
* Steeper learning curve and technical requirements

## When to Choose Each
Slack is suitable for large teams and enterprises that prioritize ease of use, scalability, and a wide range of integrations. It is ideal for teams that do not require full data ownership and control. Element, on the other hand, is perfect for small to medium-sized teams, startups, and organizations that value data sovereignty and cost-effectiveness. It is also suitable for teams with technical expertise and a desire for customization and extensibility.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data in JSON format using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to migrate your Slack data to Element.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and settings in Element.
5. Test and verify that all data and functionality have been successfully migrated.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its technical requirements and limited user support. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's scalability is dependent on the self-hosted server, which can be a bottleneck for large teams. However, for teams that value data sovereignty and cost-effectiveness, Element is a viable alternative to Slack, and we recommend switching to Element if you have the technical expertise and resources to support it.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not require a wide range of integrations
* Startups that prioritize data ownership and control
* Technical teams that can handle the setup and maintenance of an Element server
* Organizations with limited budgets that cannot afford Slack's per-user costs
* Teams that do not require mobile apps for on-the-go access

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, with no per-user costs.
### Is Element as scalable as Slack?
No, Element's scalability is dependent on the self-hosted server, which can be a bottleneck for large teams.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools and services?
Yes, Element has native integration with the Matrix protocol and can be integrated with other tools and services using APIs and webhooks.
### Is Element suitable for large enterprises?
Not yet, due to its technical requirements and limited user support.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data in JSON format and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for teams, offering real-time messaging, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison benefits teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, primarily due to concerns over data ownership, cost, or specific feature requirements. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data or reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but Mattermost's self-hosted option gives teams more flexibility in terms of customizing their infrastructure.
* Integration with GitHub: Mattermost has native integration with GitHub, allowing for more seamless development workflows, while Slack requires a third-party integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Strong support for mobile devices
* Free version available for small teams
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option gives teams full control over their data
* Customizable and extensible through plugins and APIs
* Strong support for development workflows through GitHub integration
* Free and open-source
* Can be more complex to set up and manage, especially for non-technical teams

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations with third-party apps. It's well-suited for small to medium-sized teams that don't require a high level of customization or control over their data. On the other hand, Mattermost is a good choice for teams that require a high level of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing their own server. This is particularly well-suited for large teams or enterprises with specific security and compliance requirements.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool like Slack Exporter.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either on your own infrastructure or through a cloud provider like AWS or Google Cloud.
3. Use the Mattermost API or a tool like matterbridge to import your Slack data into Mattermost.
4. Configure your Mattermost server to meet your team's specific needs, including setting up plugins and integrations.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready platform for teams that require a high level of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing their own server. However, one specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's mobile apps are not as polished as Slack's, which can be a drawback for teams that rely heavily on mobile devices. Overall, we recommend Mattermost for teams that require a high level of customization and control over their data, while Slack is a better choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't require a high level of customization and are looking for a free, self-hosted option.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that are currently using Slack's free plan and are looking to reduce costs.
* Large teams (more than 50 users) that require a high level of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing their own server.
* Teams that require a high level of customization and extensibility through plugins and APIs.
* Teams that are already using GitHub and are looking for a more seamless development workflow.

## FAQ
### Is Mattermost free?
Yes, Mattermost is free and open-source, with a self-hosted option available.
### Can I use Mattermost with my existing Slack integrations?
Some Slack integrations may not be compatible with Mattermost, but many can be replicated using Mattermost's API or plugins.
### Is Mattermost as easy to use as Slack?
No, Mattermost can be more complex to set up and manage, especially for non-technical teams.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, you can export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool and then import it into Mattermost.
### Is Mattermost available on mobile devices?
Yes, Mattermost has mobile apps available for both iOS and Android, but they are not as polished as Slack's.

* Cost: Discord offers a free plan with limitations, while Element is free and self-hosted.
* Data Ownership: Element allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Discord's data ownership is subject to its terms of service.
* Setup Complexity: Discord has a more straightforward setup process, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Element is highly scalable due to its self-hosted nature, whereas Discord's scalability is limited by its proprietary infrastructure.

| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|

* Large community and user base
* Easy to use and set up
* Cross-platform compatibility
* Rich media support

* Self-hosted and open-source

# Notion vs AppFlowy

## Overview

Notion is a popular all-in-one workspace combining notes, wikis, databases, and project management. AppFlowy is an open-source alternative with a local-first architecture that keeps your data on your device or own server.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; AppFlowy is completely free
- **Data location**: AppFlowy stores data locally by default; Notion stores on their servers
- **Offline support**: AppFlowy works fully offline; Notion requires internet for most features
- **Privacy**: AppFlowy does not collect usage data; Notion privacy policy allows data analysis
- **Feature parity**: Notion has more polished features and AI tools; AppFlowy is rapidly catching up

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | AppFlowy |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### AppFlowy

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy](https://github.com/AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy) * ~59k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion suits teams wanting a polished workspace with AI writing tools and seamless collaboration without managing infrastructure.

**Choose AppFlowy if:** AppFlowy is ideal for privacy-conscious individuals, users in regions with data sovereignty requirements, or anyone needing offline-first functionality.

## Migration Path

Export your Notion workspace as Markdown plus CSV files, then import the Markdown files into AppFlowy. Database structures will need to be recreated manually.

## Our Take

AppFlowy is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your AppFlowy instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted AppFlowy will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is AppFlowy free to use?
Yes. AppFlowy is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to AppFlowy?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the AppFlowy import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does AppFlowy get regular updates?
Yes. AppFlowy has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use AppFlowy without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if AppFlowy development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [AppFlowy](https://appflowy.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: AppFlowy is a free, self-hosted alternative to Notion. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

Notion, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams that want a user-friendly interface and are willing to pay for it. It's also a good option for teams that need to integrate with many third-party apps and want a robust feature set.

title: GitHub vs GitLab
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control platforms used for software development, offering a range of tools and services to manage code repositories, collaborate on projects, and track changes. This comparison is beneficial for developers, teams, and organizations looking to choose between the two or considering switching from one to the other, particularly for those seeking more control over their data or looking for a self-hosted solution.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free accounts with limited features, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted version with more features.
* Data ownership: GitLab provides more control over data ownership, especially with its self-hosted option.
* Setup complexity: GitHub is generally easier to set up, especially for individual users or small teams.
* Scalability: GitLab is more scalable, particularly for large teams or enterprises, due to its self-hosting capabilities.
* Integration with CI/CD pipelines: GitLab has a built-in CI/CD tool, while GitHub relies on third-party integrations like GitHub Actions.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Limited control over data ownership
**GitLab:**
* Offers a free self-hosted version with more features
* Provides more control over data ownership
* Highly scalable and customizable
* Has a built-in CI/CD tool
* Can be complex to set up, especially for self-hosting

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams or individual developers who prioritize ease of use and a large community of users. It's also a good option for those who don't need a high level of control over their data or don't require advanced features like self-hosting. On the other hand, GitLab is suitable for larger teams or enterprises that require a high level of scalability, customization, and control over their data. It's also a good option for those who want a self-hosted solution and are willing to invest time and resources into setting it up.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub export tool, which creates a `.git` archive.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab and navigate to the "New project" page.
3. Click on "Import project" and select "GitHub" as the import source.
4. Follow the prompts to authenticate with GitHub and select the repository you want to import.
5. Wait for the import process to complete, which may take several minutes depending on the size of your repository.

## Our Take
GitLab is a production-ready alternative to GitHub for most users, offering a range of features and a high level of customizability. However, one technical limitation worth noting is that GitLab's self-hosted version can be complex to set up and require significant resources, especially for large teams or enterprises. Overall, we recommend switching to GitLab if you're a team or organization that values control over your data, scalability, and customization, and is willing to invest time and resources into setting it up.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of 10-20 developers who want more control over their data and are willing to self-host
* Medium-sized teams of 50-100 developers who require advanced features like CI/CD pipelines and scalability
* Large enterprises with 200+ developers who need a highly customizable and scalable solution
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and security
* Developers who want a free self-hosted solution with more features than GitHub's free plan

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
GitLab offers a free self-hosted version, as well as a free plan with limited features on its cloud platform.
### Can I self-host GitHub?
No, GitHub does not offer self-hosting options.
### Is GitLab as easy to use as GitHub?
No, GitLab can be more complex to set up, especially for self-hosting, but it offers more advanced features and customization options.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to GitLab?
Yes, you can migrate your GitHub repository to GitLab using the import tool.
### Does GitLab have a large community of users?
Yes, GitLab has a large and growing community of users, although it's still smaller than GitHub's.
